name: Uma Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the Harlow estate, have done for nineteen years. It's a big place, 400 hectares, about 250 beef cattle and a lot of potatoes. I'm the stock person, so I check the cattle first thing, sort feed, move groups between fields, and in autumn I'm on the potato harvester like everyone else. The family who own it are decent enough. Mr Harlow's son runs it now and he's keener on figures than his father was.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The potato harvest, every year. Twelve-hour days in the dust for six weeks. My partner Tom drives a delivery van for the builders' merchant, and with Elsa at fourteen and Finn at ten, somebody's always needing a lift somewhere. I don't touch any of that AI stuff. I've got enough on with the phone the estate gave me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every few years there's something that's going to change farming forever and mostly it doesn't. I'd say it in the tea room and that's about it, I don't post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things stay as they are, and that's fine by me. I know my job, I know my cattle, and I've got a steady wage. If young Mr Harlow buys some clever software for the office, that's his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. We'd keep putting a bit by each month, about 100, and keep chipping at the mortgage. Maybe this would be the year I finally fix the fence at the bottom of our own garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of the tools if the estate brought them in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd learn the bit I needed and no more. I watched the office manager spend a whole morning arguing with a computer about a cattle passport. I could have done it with a pen in five minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the estate who'd want things to change more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Mr Harlow, probably. He's always at shows looking at shiny machines. But he's also careful with money, so I don't think he'd buy anything that didn't pay for itself.

S0.say: I'm not surprised. Every few years there's something that's going to change farming forever, and mostly it doesn't.
S0.think: It means things stay as they are, and that's fine by me. I know my job and my cattle and I've got a steady wage.
S0.do: Carries on as she is, putting about 100 a month aside and chipping away at the mortgage. Might finally fix the fence at the bottom of the family garden.
S0.quote: I watched the office manager spend a whole morning arguing with a computer about a cattle passport.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is comfortable with routine and quietly sceptical of new technology. She doesn't blame or praise anyone, describing the estate owners as decent and careful. She'd learn only what she was made to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mm. That one I'd believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, there's always change and you get on with it. No point getting worked up about it in front of people. I'd probably say that to the other workers at the estate as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. Young Mr Harlow has already been looking at GPS collars that move the cattle without anyone walking them. If he buys those, half of what I do goes, and he doesn't need two stock people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job well, and I'd wait and see what the estate actually buys. We'd save a bit more, maybe 150 a month instead of 100. I suppose I'd ask around the other farms quietly, just to know what's out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A sort of nagging feeling when I'm out with the cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the other stock person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren. He's 31 and good with his phone. If it comes down to one of us, I think they'd keep the younger one who'll learn the collars. I don't blame them, I'd probably do the same in their place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get on with it, but you'd also be asking around other farms. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. You say one thing in the tea room and you do another thing at home. Tom would tell you I've been worrying about jobs since the day I started.

S1.say: It's how things go. There's always change and you get on with it, and there's no point getting worked up about it in front of people.
S1.think: Young Mr Harlow has been looking at GPS collars that move cattle without anyone walking them. If he buys those, half my job goes and he won't need two stock people.
S1.do: Keeps her head down, does her job well and waits to see what the estate buys. Raises savings from 100 to 150 a month and quietly asks around other farms about work.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a nagging feeling while out with the cattle.
S1.quote: If it comes down to one of us, I think they'd keep the younger one who'll learn the collars.
S1.fieldNote: Uma's public calm hides a specific fear: GPS cattle collars and a younger colleague. She refuses to blame her employer and sees it as plain business. She admits openly to saying one thing in the tea room and another at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? Both of us? Tom drives a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably something like everyone's in the same boat, which is what people say when they've got nothing else. I wouldn't be posting anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means we're both out of work around the same time. Robots on the estate, robot vans for the builders' merchant. I've got no other skills on paper, I've never used a computer for anything, and four months of savings doesn't go far with two kids and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing would be to stop every bit of spending we don't need, so no school trip for Elsa, no new football boots for Finn. I'd ask my sister, who has a bit more, if we could borrow from her if it came to it. And I'd go to the job centre and the bank about the mortgage, though I wouldn't know what to ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I'd feel like the floor's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Elsa about the school trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, because she'd see through anything else. She'd be upset for a day and then she'd tell me it didn't matter, which would be worse. She's a good kid like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at all that might make it easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the government did something quick, like money for people who lose their jobs to this. I'm not one for handouts as a rule, but if it's everyone at once, that's different. Without that, I don't see a way through for us.

S2.say: Everyone's in the same boat, which is what people say when they've got nothing else to say. I wouldn't be posting anything about it.
S2.think: Tom and I would both be out of work around the same time, me to robots on the estate and him to robot vans. I've got no other skills on paper, and four months of savings doesn't go far with two kids and a mortgage.
S2.do: Stops all spending that isn't needed, including Elsa's school trip and Finn's new football boots. Asks her sister about borrowing money and goes to the job centre and the bank about the mortgage.
S2.feel: Panicked, as if the floor has gone.
S2.quote: I'd tell her the truth, because she'd see through anything else. She'd be upset for a day and then she'd tell me it didn't matter, which would be worse.
S2.fieldNote: Uma's situation stacks up fast: both household incomes exposed, no transferable skills she can name and only a few months of savings. She has no plan beyond cutting costs and leaning on family. She'd accept government help in a crisis despite disliking handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should start preparing, which is easy to say. I'd tell the younger ones on the estate to learn the machines. For me, I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still lose the job, just later. Five years doesn't make me a different person. I'd be 48 with nothing on paper but nineteen, well, twenty-four years of cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd build our savings as hard as we could, maybe 250 a month by cutting the second car and holidays. I'd talk to Tom about which of us looks for something steadier first. And I'd make sure Elsa takes her school exams seriously, because she'll be leaving school right when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Less of a shock, more of a slow dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years you felt the floor going. What does the extra time change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives us time to stack up some money, and that matters. But it doesn't give me a new job. I think I'd spend five years watching it come closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about any training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it. Whether I'd go is another thing. I left school at sixteen and the agricultural course was the last classroom I sat in, and I didn't enjoy that one.

S3.say: People should start preparing, which is easy to say. I'd tell the younger ones on the estate to learn the machines and keep quiet about myself.
S3.think: I'd still lose the job, just later, because five years doesn't make me a different person. I'd be 48 with nothing on paper but years of cattle.
S3.do: Builds savings as fast as possible, about 250 a month, by giving up the second car and holidays. Talks with Tom about who looks for steadier work first and makes sure Elsa takes her exams seriously.
S3.feel: Alarmed, more slow dread than shock.
S3.quote: I think I'd spend five years watching it come closer.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time helps Uma's savings but not her sense of options. She's reluctant to retrain and remembers disliking the classroom. Her daughter's timing, leaving school as AGI arrives, becomes a new focus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Finn would be twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so don't panic. I'd say that at work and to my sister. It sounds sensible, doesn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is easier for me than for the kids. I'd probably keep my job most of that time, because the estate won't buy robots until they're cheap and proven. But Elsa and Finn would be starting out right when it all arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving, about 150 a month, and I'd pay the mortgage down when I could. I'd wait and see what the estate does before I think about anything new for myself. Mostly I'd be pushing the kids towards something solid, maybe a trade or nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but mostly for the kids, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a trade or nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you need people for those, or I think you do. Then again, you've just told me robots can do hands-on work too. So I don't really know what to tell them, and that's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your own work in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I'm good at what I do and I'd like to finish my years doing it. If they bring the collars in, I'll learn what I have to.

S4.say: There's time, so don't panic. It sounds sensible when I say it at work or to my sister.
S4.think: Ten years is easier for me than for the kids. I'd likely keep my job most of that time, but Elsa and Finn would be starting out just as it all arrives.
S4.do: Keeps saving about 150 a month and pays down the mortgage when possible. Waits to see what the estate does and steers the children towards something solid like a trade or nursing.
S4.feel: Anxious, mostly on her children's behalf.
S4.quote: So I don't really know what to tell them, and that's the honest answer.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Uma's worry shifts almost entirely to her children. She expects the estate to be slow to buy robots, which protects her own job. She catches herself giving career advice that the scenario itself undercuts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tom and I would both be out of work at once with nowhere to go. What would help is money from the government to tide families over, quickly, and someone telling me plainly what jobs there'd be for someone like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the cattle would think. I know that sounds daft. But I've got a cow called Biscuit who follows me round the field, and no collar's going to get that.

headlineQuote: I've got a cow called Biscuit who follows me round the field, and no collar's going to get that.
portrait: Uma Jensen, 43, has been the stock person on the large Harlow estate for nineteen years, working with beef cattle and potatoes. She never uses AI and prefers to keep her head down, blaming no one and treating change as plain business. She's calm if AI stalls and uneasy about GPS collars and a younger colleague under steady change. Fast AGI leaves her panicked because both her and her partner's jobs would go at once; with more time her worry moves to her children starting out.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her partner would both lose their jobs at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Quick government money to tide families over, and someone telling her plainly what work would exist for someone like her.
